ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Surgical Oncology Consultation — Bob Marley

code.originalText: Biopsy result: acral melanoma of the toe; surgical oncology consultation, staging, and a shared decision about surgery

text.paragraph: Suspected subungual melanoma of the right great toe in a 32-year-old musician and footballer with dark skin: a brown-black band about 5 mm wide that has not grown out in two months, with pigment on the proximal nail fold. A full-thickness nail matrix biopsy is booked with our dermatologist this week. Please see him with the result to advise on staging and definitive surgery. [S]
Urgency: Urgent, within two weeks, with the biopsy result. [S]

list.item: If the biopsy confirms melanoma, what is its stage, and what staging tests does he need?
Should he be offered a sentinel lymph node biopsy?
What are the surgical options, and is a digit-sparing operation safe for him, given what matters to him?
Will he need treatment after surgery, and how should he be followed?
How should he check his own skin and nails from now on?

text.paragraph: Mr. Marley, 32, is seen at the request of Dr. Clarke with the result of a nail matrix biopsy taken two days after his first visit. He noticed a dark band in his right great toenail about two months ago after a knock at football; it did not grow out, and pigment spread onto the nail fold. He is otherwise well, takes no medicines, and has had no previous operations. He is a touring musician who runs and plays football several times a week. He told me that his faith, his music and his football all matter to him in this decision, and that he would like to keep the toe if that can be done without lowering his chance of cure. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Robert Nesta Marley was born on February 6, 1945, at Nine Mile in Saint Ann Parish, Jamaica, the son of a Jamaican mother and a white English father. [D]
He was a Jamaican singer, songwriter and musician, considered one of the pioneers of reggae, who toured the world with his band, the Wailers. [D]
He was raised a Roman Catholic and converted to Rastafari in the late 1960s; he became known as a Rastafarian icon who infused his music with spirituality. [D]

In 1977 he noticed a pigmented lesion on the nail bed of his right great toe and thought it was the result of a football injury. The first physician he saw thought that a reasonable explanation; because the lesion was growing, he saw a second physician, who performed a biopsy. [D]

Whether the football injury caused the lesion is disputed: an encyclopedia article states that the lesion was not caused by the injury but was a sign of a cancer already present, and clinicians note that many people with acral melanoma recall an injury to the site, while the role of trauma is not established. [R]

list.item: Acral lentiginous melanoma of the right great toe nail unit, clinical stage IB (cT1b N0 M0) (C43.71). A thin invasive acral melanoma of the nail unit, T1b by the AJCC 8th edition because it is 0.8 mm thick, with no clinical sign of spread: clinical stage IB. No scans or blood tests are needed at this stage. The chance that a sentinel node contains melanoma is about 5 to 10 percent, so a sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered; it gives the most accurate stage, which decides whether treatment after surgery would be considered. There are two surgical choices. Amputation at the interphalangeal joint has the lowest chance of the melanoma returning in the toe. Digit-sparing en bloc excision of the whole nail unit down to the bone, with a 5 to 10 mm margin and a full-thickness skin graft, keeps the toe and its function; for melanomas this thin, published series show similar survival, with a higher chance (in some series about one in five) of a local recurrence that would then be treated by amputation. Either is oncologically appropriate for him; it is his decision, and his wish to keep the toe for his faith, his music and his football is a sound reason to choose the digit-sparing operation. If the excision showed a thicker melanoma or involved margins, I would recommend amputation. Adjuvant immunotherapy is considered only from stage IIB, so it is not expected to be needed unless the sentinel node is positive. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Clarke's intake note. Dermoscopy by the clinic's dermatologist: a brown-black band about 5 mm wide with longitudinal lines irregular in color, thickness and spacing, and pigment on the proximal nail fold and hyponychium. Full-thickness excisional nail matrix biopsy: acral lentiginous melanoma, Breslow thickness 0.8 mm, not ulcerated, mitotic rate 1 per mm2, no lymphovascular or perineural invasion, no microsatellites, with melanoma in situ at the lateral edges of the specimen. [S]

list.item: Lymphoscintigraphy and right inguinal sentinel lymph node biopsy, with the definitive operation, in two weeks. [S]

Definitive surgery by his choice: digit-sparing en bloc excision of the nail unit down to the bone with a 5 to 10 mm margin and a full-thickness skin graft from the inner upper arm; amputation at the interphalangeal joint if the margins are involved or the melanoma proves thicker. [S]
No staging CT, PET, or LDH for clinical stage IB without symptoms; no blood tests needed before surgery. [S]

No adjuvant therapy if the sentinel node is negative; surveillance with history and examination of the skin, nails, graft and nodes every 6 to 12 months for 5 years and then yearly, with a yearly full skin examination by dermatology. [S]
Monthly skin self-examination, including the palms, soles, between the toes and all nails, the graft, and both groins, taught after surgery. [S]
A stiff-soled shoe until the graft heals, then a graded return to running and football. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Clarke, who sees him the same day. The choices were explained with drawings and a written summary; Mr. Marley chose the digit-sparing operation with a sentinel node biopsy and agreed in advance to amputation if the pathology required it. He decides who else receives this note. [S]
Follow-up: Surgery in two weeks; surgical review of the graft at one and six weeks; Dr. Clarke continues primary care and surveillance. [S]
